title: Security teams urged to center defense on the flaw profile attackers target most
raw_text: Attackers are increasingly focusing on a limited range of critical vulnerabilities to run attacks with flaws packaged into exploits within as little as three days. Rapid7’s latest Quarterly Threat Landscape report found the number of newly exploited vulnerabilities in Q3 of 2026 was 43, up 19% year on year. Douglas McKee, director of vulnerability intelligence at Rapid7, said it would be wrong to interpret that 19% as indication of a “slow, steady climb in exploitation,” however. “New high-severity CVEs, the ones rated 7 through 10, are up 133% year over year, and publicly available proof-of-concept code is up around 86% over the same stretch,” said McKee. “So the pile of things that could be exploited is growing far faster than the set of things attackers are actually choosing to exploit.” Expedited exploit production line Rapid7 also found that the majority of underground forum posts referenced CVEs already in vendor advisories or in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog within days of disclosure. This indicates rapid commercial repackaging of known flaws rather than a wave of genuinely novel zero-day sales, according to Rapid7. “AI tooling is surfacing flaws quicker than any team can realistically triage them, but adversaries are still being picky about which ones they pick up and weaponize,” McKee said. Attackers exploited select high-severity flaws within an average of three days, with 71% of the exploitation tracked by Rapid7 landing within a week. Vulnerabilities that require no authentication and little or no user interaction are favored for remote exploitation. Defenders need to adapt to a world where high-severity flaws are packaged into exploits in days rather than weeks. “Once a new high-severity flaw goes public, you’ve got roughly 72 hours before someone is using it in the wild, and attackers aren’t casting a wide net while they do it,” said McKee. The profile attackers target most These days attackers are shopping in one aisle: remote, unauthenticated, and zero-click exploits. Rapid7’s study found that nearly 80% of what got exploited this quarter could be reached remotely, with no login required and nothing for the victim to click . “If your patching cadence still has the word ‘monthly’ in it, you’re defending against an adversary who abandoned that schedule a long time ago,” McKee warned. Rather than attempting to patch everything faster , security teams should prioritize patching based on risk management questions and issues specific to their environments. Given attackers’ current preferences, security leaders should identify systems that are exposed to that remote, unauthenticated, zero-click attacking profile, and consider how many days of exposure they are willing to accept on each of them. Concern over AI-orchestrated attacks rising CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that AI-enabled attacks tops the list of security leaders’ threat concerns, with 45% of CISOs rating their concern high. But in terms of what Rapid7 found, artificial intelligence showed up as an operational component in only about 8% of the attacks it tracked. “It was running the tactical middle of the attack, choosing the next technique or triaging which targets were worth the effort,” McKee said of attacker AI use uncovered by Rapid7. “It wasn’t deciding who to go after or why. A human still made that call.” Still, other security experts warn of a growing wave of AI-orchestrated attacks. Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense, said that Russian APT groups are already running AI-powered attacks, and predicted more are coming. Russian and other APT group attackers often use Chinese models such as DeepSeek — which has few constraints or guardrails — and are often able to switch between models in running attacks, he said. Tymoshyk added that by running agentic attacks hackers can draw on a deeper pool of technical knowledge — expertise in database admin, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — than can be commonly achieved by conventional human-only attack teams. Human teams tend to consist of various individuals that specialize in specific technical skills such as web app security or malware development, whereas abusing agentic tools gives attackers ready access to multi-skilled entities that they might not be able to easily recruit in human form.

title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute credential-stealing malware
raw_text: Hackers hijacked the software release pipeline of LiteLLM, a popular open-source AI gateway, to distribute credential-stealing malware, marking the project’s second supply chain compromise this year despite security measures introduced after an earlier attack. The compromised version, 1.107.0, was distributed through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and official Docker images on October 21. LiteLLM said the malicious Python packages remained available for approximately two hours before being removed, while the affected Docker images were withdrawn or replaced later that day. The affected Docker images included those distributed under the latest, main-latest, and main-stable tags, extending the risk to deployments that pulled those tags during the exposure window. According to cybersecurity firm Aikido , files bundled with the compromised package executed automatically when Python started, even if an application did not import LiteLLM. The malware was designed to collect sensitive information from infected systems, including cloud credentials and API keys stored in LiteLLM’s database, potentially giving attackers access to services beyond the affected AI gateway. The compromised package also contained a remote access trojan that launched a background process to retrieve and execute code from attacker-controlled infrastructure every hour, according to Aikido. This could allow attackers to continue executing commands on infected systems after the initial credential theft. In its incident report, LiteLLM said attackers used stolen GitHub credentials associated with three developer accounts to manipulate its software release pipeline. The stolen credentials enabled changes to the release workflow, which was redirected to an attacker-controlled lookalike repository. The company said the attackers may have obtained the credentials from logs associated with an internet-facing internal LiteLLM deployment. It also identified circumstances in which Claude Code could expose GitHub authentication tokens in responses subsequently recorded by LiteLLM. However, it has not been established how the attackers initially accessed the deployment. LiteLLM said the incident had been contained and that customers using its private enterprise registry were unaffected. It advised organizations running the compromised open-source software to treat their environments as potentially breached and rotate exposed credentials rather than relying solely on removing the malicious package. Broader enterprise exposure “A compromised LiteLLM gateway provides a strong foothold to hackers and could expose far more than AI API keys,” said Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis. Aikido noted that the malware targeted Kubernetes service account tokens and secrets associated with CI/CD systems , including GitLab and Jenkins. The extent of any subsequent compromise may depend on the privileges assigned to the affected deployment and the credentials available to it. “An AI gateway is privileged enterprise infrastructure,” said Sakshi Grover , research director for information and data security at IDC. “Centralizing access to multiple models can improve governance, but it also concentrates trust.” Beyond credential theft, a compromised gateway could disrupt business applications that depend on it, Grover said. IDC’s Future Enterprise Resiliency and Spending Survey, conducted in July 2026, found that 95% of enterprises surveyed worldwide had at least one company-funded agent-enabled workflow in production. A wider incident response challenge The malware’s remote access component could remain active even after the compromised package is removed, complicating efforts to determine whether an affected system is safe to restore. “CISOs should not treat this just as a package-cleanup exercise,” Prabhu said. He recommended identifying deployments running affected packages or container images, isolating suspected systems, and preserving forensic evidence before rebuilding them using trusted software. Grover warned that security teams should avoid launching Python or pip in suspected compromised environments because the malware’s startup hooks could execute again. She recommended identifying affected packages and container image digests across production environments, developer systems and CI runners. “Missing indicators do not prove an environment is clean,” Grover said. Prabhu recommended examining logs for evidence of persistent access or misuse of stolen credentials. He said organizations should rotate every secret accessible to the compromised deployment, including credentials associated with cloud infrastructure and development pipelines. Grover also recommended linking AI usage telemetry with cloud and identity audit logs to help identify possible credential misuse. Unusual token consumption could provide an indication of unauthorized activity, although attackers may avoid generating noticeable increases in spending, she said. Software supply chain weaknesses In March, malicious versions of LiteLLM’s Python package were distributed following a compromise that the project linked to the Trivy security scanner used in its software release pipeline. After this, LiteLLM strengthened its software release process by moving releases to a private repository and introducing signed Docker images. However, attackers used stolen GitHub credentials to modify the release workflow, which then signed and published the malicious software, the company said. The incident shows how malicious code can pass through an authorized software signing process when attackers compromise the release pipeline. A valid digital signature can verify that an artifact has not been altered since signing, but cannot establish whether the code was safe when it was signed. “Repeated supply-chain compromises show that a trusted source repository does not guarantee that the package users install was built from that source,” Prabhu said. Prabhu recommended cryptographically signed releases backed by verifiable build provenance, alongside stronger protection of publishing credentials. Grover said enterprises should also inspect distributed software packages and container images before deployment, rather than relying solely on the integrity of the source repository. She recommended restricting production deployments to verified package and image digests and requiring independent approval for changes to release workflows.

The compromised version, 1.107.0, was distributed through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and official Docker images on October 21. LiteLLM said the malicious Python packages remained available for approximately two hours before being removed, while the affected Docker images were withdrawn or replaced later that day. The affected Docker images included those distributed under the latest, main-latest, and main-stable tags, extending the risk to deployments that pulled those tags during the exposure window.

title: China-linked hackers used agentic AI in attack on 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants
raw_text: A China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used an open-source agentic AI framework to turn its stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft said. Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the activity to Storm-0940, which it said has used the ARTEX framework since as early as September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations. In some cases, the group gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting a victim. Microsoft said the activity did not result from a compromise of or vulnerability in its own systems, products, or services. “This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially,” Microsoft said in a blog post. Machine-speed sign-ins Following the breach at ConnectWise, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 attempts per minute, the post added. ConnectWise published an initial advisory on October 16 covering attempted unauthorized access associated with its Cloud Backup product, and later expanded its containment guidance. The attackers used the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications to authenticate to Microsoft 365 environments through apps that had already been granted access. That removed the need for interactive user sign-ins, the post said. In some environments, the agents moved on to Microsoft Graph and directory operations. These included reconnaissance, application credential changes to establish persistence, and changes to identities, groups, and privileged roles. Microsoft warned that such changes “can remain active as a backdoor” even after the original application is remediated. ConnectWise did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yih Khai Wong, senior research manager for security services at IDC Asia/Pacific, said the timeline is beyond the reach of human response. “2,900 sign-in attempts per minute and gaining privileged cloud access in under three hours is not a timeline any human analyst queue can keep up with, no matter how well-staffed the SOC,” Wong said. He said containment actions such as disabling credentials, revoking tokens and isolating service principals should trigger automatically on predefined thresholds, with humans reviewing them afterward. In the face of machine-speed attacks, he added, “relying on a human to click ‘approve’ will not cut it.” Trusted apps, untrusted access Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said the incident exposes a gap in how enterprises secure access. “Companies spend enormous amounts of time securing employee logins with MFA and conditional access, while third-party applications can hold equally powerful permissions and authenticate without any employee being involved,” Kadakia said. “We’ve spent years implementing zero trust for humans while continuing to implicitly trust machines.” He said vendor integrations should be treated like privileged accounts, with minimum permissions, continuous monitoring, periodic access reviews, and a tested way to revoke access. “An application you stopped using a year ago may still have permissions in your environment today,” Kadakia added. Wong said accountability is shared. “ConnectWise, as the entry point, is responsible for protecting the credentials and infrastructure that let its app reach across tenants,” he said, adding that customers are responsible for knowing what access they granted, to whom, and for how long. Commoditized attack tooling ARTEX is a Chinese open-source multi-agent LLM system that can use any AI model. Its agents run a penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little human interaction. Microsoft said public reporting in October linked the framework to data breaches at Korean financial institutions and that actors across multiple regions are using it. Storm-0940 has been active since 2021, Microsoft said. Its ARTEX-driven targeting spans aerospace and defense, energy, financial services, government, semiconductor and technology, among other sectors. Most of the targeting was unsuccessful, the company said, but the group achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a short time. “Attacks are being commoditized; threat actors are increasingly turning to open-source tools to launch attacks, meaning the operational sophistication once reserved for well-resourced groups is now available to anyone who can run a GitHub repo against an LLM API,” Wong said. Kadakia said there is no reliable way to tell an AI agent from a human operator by examining individual requests. A legitimate API call made with stolen credentials looks the same regardless of who initiated it, he said. “Defenders should focus on what the identity is doing, not whether a human or AI is controlling it,” he said. Disable ConnectWise connections Microsoft advised customers to keep affected ConnectWise connections disabled until ConnectWise issues restoration instructions and not to delete enterprise applications as a first step. Organizations should search tenants by the four affected application IDs rather than display names and preserve Entra, Purview, and SIEM records, the company said. It also urged a review of activity from at least October 15, extending back to October 1 where records allow. The company also cautioned against treating exposure as proof of a breach. “The presence of an affected application, or even successful authentication, does not necessarily indicate unauthorized data access or data exfiltration,” Microsoft said in the post.
summary: A China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used an open-source agentic AI framework to turn its stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft said. Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the activity to Storm-0940, which it said has used the ARTEX framework since as early as September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations. In some cases, the group gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting a victim. Microsoft said the activity did not result from a compromise of or vulnerability in its own systems, products, or services.

title: Microsoft Frontier Tour London: Agentic AI governance in the spotlight
raw_text:
During the opening keynote at the company’s Frontier Tour event in London, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella discussed how the company would be addressing the growing concern of tokenomics.

Analyst Gartner has predicted that by 2030, a failure to adopt adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) governance runtime controls will triple the cost of AI deployments, eroding value. It warned that standard cloud billing alerts are a lagging indicator of overspending.

In its Cost governance is a non-negotiable addition to AI governance report, Gartner said: “Relying on these escalations hours or days after overspending has been identified delays mitigation and fails to prevent immediate curtailing of runaway inference costs at runtime.”

Discussing how Microsoft would be tackling potential runaway costs associated with overuse of AI inference, Nadella spoke about a Microsoft project that provides AI model orchestration, enabling organisations to select a model, either run locally or in the public cloud.

“We now have HydraFusion, which is a learned model where you are now able to take advantage of powerful local models or an RTX Spark,” he said. “You now have very capable coding models. You can start using HyperFusion whenever a task or one of the sub-agents of a task can be done and can be satisfied by using just a local model.”

According to Nadella, this means IT departments can essentially provide “an infinite token factory”.

The company made Project HydraFusion available on GitHub in September as a research preview. The project’s goal is to deliver what Microsoft describes as “frontier intelligence through runtime orchestration”. In the GitHub post, Microsoft said HydraFusion creates a full execution plan, choosing from models across multiple providers to draft, critique and revise, or cascade to more powerful models to complete a task.

  • Who is the boss of an AI agent: AI agents that work for an employee, a business process or the enterprise carry different risks and deliver different returns, and organisations that govern them all the same way stand to get both wrong.
  • Why AI agents cannot be trusted to secure agentic AI yet: The idea of using AI agents to secure AI agents seems compelling, but in doing so, we risk unnecessarily expanding our attack surface.

Along with demos of the tools Microsoft offers for developing agentic AI, Nadella used the opening keynote to discuss how Microsoft was addressing AI trust. “It starts with having a set of principles of your trust system,” he said. “I describe them as principles of observability and governance, but you need to identify every agent and you need to be able to log every activity of these agents.”

Nadella said that when an AI agent uses an AI model, it is necessary to log its chain of thought in a human-readable form. This log needs to show that the agent has complied with the organisation’s governance and compliance rules. Given that multiple AI agents may be required to complete a task, each one needs to be uniquely identifiable.

Nadella also discussed how Microsoft Agent 365 provides the agentic AI control plane for IT operations teams. He said Agent 365 “holds every agent identified, and manages and governs their policies”. According to Nadella, it also supports security operations and the budgeting requirements for FinOps.

He described how AI agents could work internally in an enterprise, where some work as penetration testers to attack enterprise IT systems, while others are tasked with fixing the security holes identified.

“You now have red agents that are continuously simulating the attacks, and you have blue agents that are continuously defending,” said Nadella. “Then you have green agents that are continuously remediating the vulnerabilities they find.”

title: Can Britain’s grid keep up with the datacentre boom?
raw_text:
Ramping datacentre demand is putting a new kind of pressure on the UK’s energy grid. Developers are jostling for position in an increasingly saturated connection queue as new facility plans arrive faster than the network that must accommodate them can grow.

Supporting this wave of infrastructure requires major investment in cabling, substations and transmission capacity. In August, for example, the National Grid announced its North West London Upgrade, a £1bn project that will connect five new datacentres across Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and London, with 1GW of electricity demand.

That project illustrates a wider shift across the country. As digital demand grows, the financial pressure to connect new infrastructure is felt by developers – and potentially by consumers too – while the need for new substations, cables and transmission capacity looks likely to reshape Britain’s digital geography as it pushes datacentre development to locations where power is available.

In this article, we look at whether Britain’s grid can keep up with the datacentre boom. We examine the sheer scale of the transmission and substation build now required, the speculative connection queue that is pushing developers north, and the increasingly urgent question of who pays for it all – the developers racing to connect, or the households whose bills ultimately fund the network.

Anatomy of a £1bn grid upgrade

The North West London Upgrade shows just how much physical infrastructure is needed to accommodate new datacentre facilities.

The project will see the installation of around 60km of new high-voltage cable, 35km of re-cabling between Sundon and Elstree, and upgrades to more than 200km of overhead lines. At Elstree, the agency is also extending an existing 400kV substation, and building a new 132kV substation at Letchmore Heath to connect the new datacentres.

The upgrade is only one part of a much bigger programme of investment in Britain’s electricity network. Ofgem’s RIIO-3 price control, for example, includes up to £10.7bn for electricity transmission between 2026 and 2031, with flexible mechanisms potentially taking investment to as much as £90bn as projects mature.

Elisabeth Cremona, energy infrastructure lead at energy think tank Ember, tells Computer Weekly that the scale of investment is a response to the unprecedented speed at which these new facilities come online.

“Datacentres represent a huge load,” she says. “You’re essentially looking at putting 500,000 houses on the grid in a single location really, really fast, and that’s just never happened before. Households don’t come online that fast, factories don’t come online that fast.”

Typically, says Cremona, building out or upgrading a grid takes between five and 15 years, while a datacentre can be ready to come online in 18 months. Bringing datacentres online quickly is also fast becoming a competitive advantage for businesses.

“Developers are behaving differently to any previous class of large energy user,” she says. “Rather than wait patiently in established queues, they’re moving to find loopholes, to find a place where they can connect immediately.”

For years, the UK’s datacentre industry has been heavily concentrated around London and the M4 corridor, driven by proximity to customers, existing fibre networks, established datacentre ecosystems and access to major business markets.

Now, with increased onus on speedy connection times and a backlog of connection requests, projects are shifting north.

Analysis of data from construction project information provider Barbour ABI finds that of the UK’s top 10 datacentre projects, only one – at East Havering in Essex – is in the London area. The remainder, totalling just under 4GW, are spread north from Oxfordshire to Lincolnshire, North Wales, the north-east and Scotland.

A changing grid landscape

According to Ofgem, connection offers rose from 41GW to 125GW between November 2024 and June 2025, with datacentres accounting for at least 80GW of that demand. Connection wait times have stretched as a result, some by as much as 15 years.

Part of the backlog is self-inflicted. Developers, aware of how slow the process is, submit multiple speculative applications for the same site to see which clears first, and that creates “zombie applications”.

Ofgem has proposed reforms intended to remove speculative and non-viable projects from the queue. Large datacentre developers would have to pay an upfront commitment fee when accepting a connection offer, which would range from £237,500 to £712,500 per megawatt. The fee would be refunded when a project reaches energisation but forfeited if it leaves the queue early.

Developers would also have to demonstrate that projects are commercially and technically ready to progress.

Matt Salter, global head of datacentres at Onnec, says the proposals reflect how tight the market has become.

“Ofgem’s ‘Pay to Stay’ proposals are a sign of just how tight the UK’s datacentre power market has become,” he tells Computer Weekly. “Asking developers to prove projects are real and ready to move makes sense, but it adds another pressure point for operators already being pushed to build faster.”

Research by Onnec shows that 92% of operators are compressing build timelines to keep pace with artificial intelligence (AI) demand, while 75% say speed-to-market pressure is forcing design decisions before infrastructure requirements are fully understood.

Salter says this creates the risk of adding to grid capacity without properly coordinating it with the rest of a facility’s infrastructure.

“The £1bn National Grid upgrade shows just how much investment is now needed, but more grid capacity on its own will not fix this,” he says. “Power, cooling, cabling and compute need to be planned together from day one, or we risk spending billions connecting new datacentres only to spend more fixing them after go-live.”

The issue is not unique to Britain. In March, Denmark’s grid operator suspended new connection requests after receiving roughly 60GW of applications in a country whose peak demand is around 7GW.

An increasingly common response to lengthening connection times is for developers to simply move where there is capacity.

Follow the power: One operator’s move north

For Spencer Lamb, CEO of datacentre operator Kao Data, the shift described above is already shaping investment decisions.

“Grid availability is one of the most important factors in determining when and where new datacentres are built,” he tells Computer Weekly. “If you cannot secure power within a commercially viable timeframe, it becomes extremely difficult to justify investing in a location, regardless of its other advantages.”

As a result, he says, operators are increasingly choosing sites where capacity already exists rather than waiting years for network upgrades. It is one reason Kao Data is investing £450m in a new facility in Greater Manchester. Lamb says the city region offered tech and AI research heritage, government support, a brownfield site that could be redeveloped for the benefit of the community, and a realistic timeline for power delivery.

He cautioned against reading the National Grid’s North West London Upgrade purely as a response to AI. Some substations, he says, have been in planning for many years, driven by demand for cloud, enterprise computing and digital services.

“What AI has done is accelerate the conversation and intensify pressures,” he says. “The reality is that the UK’s electricity infrastructure has been under increasing strain for some time, and significant long-term investment will be required if the country wants to maintain its position as a leading destination for datacentre and AI investment.”

Who pays for the new infrastructure?

While developers do bear some of the cost of these new infrastructure buildouts, the costs of expanding the grid are ultimately recovered through regulated network charges paid by households and businesses. So, the question of who pays for new infrastructure is increasingly significant for the public as power demand ramps up.

An Ofgem spokesperson tells Computer Weekly it is alert to the risk that “consumers should not unfairly shoulder the costs of connecting” datacentres, and that its bid to clean up the connection queue aims to mitigate this risk.

The regulator’s Demand Connections Reform programme is also designed to reduce the likelihood of consumers funding infrastructure that is ultimately not needed because projects fail to progress.

“Our recent consultation will help shape reforms that will help to ensure viable projects, including datacentres, connect faster and network costs are shared fairly,” says the spokesperson.

Concentration of datacentres also matters, with location materially affecting network costs, reinforcement requirements and connection timescales.

“If you suddenly get a massive cluster of datacentres,” says Ember’s Cremona, “the system operator has to build out a huge amount of transmission lines, substations, and all these very, very expensive things to supply them with power.”

With developers pushed to areas of less concentrated connection, she warns they run the risk of prioritising speed over everything else – including cost for businesses and consumers. Additionally, datacentres rarely draw as much power as they request, meaning bills could rise by more than the actual load justifies.

“They operate on average at around 50%,” says Cremona. “So that means you build a huge amount of transmission infrastructure, and they only use half of it. They’re not even using it fully, and you’re billed in a way that isn’t the most cost-efficient.”

Managing datacentre buildout is therefore a necessity in terms of not overwhelming the grid and in keeping costs down for the public. One solution is to make datacentre demand more flexible, though this remains a difficult pill to swallow for operators facing consumer demand for always-on cloud and enterprise workloads. Cremona says it’s still something worth aiming for, though the road to get there may be long.

“If you could enforce flexibility, developers would get online faster and you would bring down network requirements,” she says. “It’s really a win-win for everyone.”

Can the grid keep up with AI?

Britain’s datacentre ambitions are increasingly becoming an electricity infrastructure problem. The North West London Upgrade demonstrates the physical scale of investment required to connect just five datacentre facilities, while the wider connection queue shows how quickly demand is outstripping available capacity.

Asked whether the UK is doing enough to keep power availability in step with planned capacity, Kao Data’s Lamb is blunt: “In short, no.”

Too often, he says, discussions focus on securing capacity in a handful of established markets, rather than taking a more strategic view of where power is available today and how future demand can be distributed across the country.

“The remaining bottleneck is therefore not simply generation capacity itself, but the speed, transparency and coordination needed to connect demand with available power,” he says. “We need to deliver new network upgrades before the UK’s AI and economic opportunity is lost.”

title: Data readiness, not compute, seen as biggest barrier to sovereign AI in the Gulf
raw_text:
As organisations across the Gulf move artificial intelligence (AI) from pilot projects into public services and regulated industries, data readiness and operational control are becoming as important as access to computing power, according to Core42.

Mohammed Retmi, vice-president of sovereign clouds at Core42, said organisations seeking to operationalise sovereign AI must understand what data they hold, how it can be processed, and which security and governance controls must apply throughout the AI lifecycle.

“Data readiness, not compute, is the usual bottleneck,” he said. Organisations need to establish whether their data is trusted, accurate and appropriately classified before using it to train models, while applying consistent controls to prompts, generated outputs and retained information.

The challenge is particularly significant in regulated environments, where data classification determines where workloads can run and which controls must be applied. Under the UAE National Cloud Security Policy, organisations must match their infrastructure choices to their data classifications and applicable security requirements.

Core42 offers two approaches to address these requirements: its Sovereign Enabled Public Cloud, designed to support partial sovereign cloud requirements; and its Signature Private Cloud, which supports more isolated environments, including fully air-gapped deployments. The appropriate environment depends on the classification of the data, the applicable regulations and the controls that can be verified, Retmi said.

“The classification decision stays with the customer. Our job is to provide the environment and controls that match it,” he added.

Moving sovereign AI into production

Retmi identified four recurring challenges for Gulf organisations progressing from AI experimentation to production: data readiness, access to sovereign compute, integration with existing systems and operational scalability.

For organisations that need sensitive workloads to remain in-country, building dedicated AI infrastructure can involve substantial capital investment and lengthy deployment times. Core42 has sought to address this through Sovereign AI Compute, launched with e& UAE, which provides government entities and enterprises with on-demand access to in-country AI infrastructure on a consumption basis.

The offering removes the need for upfront infrastructure investment and does not charge data egress fees, according to Retmi. Integration is another concern as organisations seek to connect AI models with existing applications, data sources and security tools without having to build every integration themselves.

Core42 recently launched a partner program, bringing more than 50 independent software suppliers, technology partners and resellers onto sovereign-enabled public cloud. The platform combines Microsoft Azure’s hyperscale cloud foundation with an independent Core42 governance layer, allowing organisations to use familiar cloud technologies alongside additional sovereignty controls.

Retmi argued that organisations also need greater visibility into their AI dependencies, including the models, suppliers and infrastructure involved in processing information.

“AI strategies succeed when deployments are usable and trusted by the business that relies on them. The sophistication of the model matters far less”

Mohammed Retmi, Core42

He cited an IBM study in the UAE that found 96% of executives did not fully understand their AI dependencies. The growing use of unauthorised external AI tools, often referred to as shadow AI, can further complicate governance when employees enter sensitive information into services outside their organisation’s approved environments.

Core42 Insight is designed to provide organisations with a consolidated view of sovereignty controls and their compliance posture across these environments.

On the other hand, Core42’s sovereign-enabled public cloud, developed with the Abu Dhabi Department of Government Enablement and Microsoft, supports 47 Abu Dhabi government entities and 11 million daily digital interactions, Retmi said.

Core42 has also developed a sovereign-enabled financial cloud with the Central Bank of the UAE. Retmi said these deployments form part of the G42 Intelligence Grid, which is designed to deliver computing capacity at scale. “AI strategies succeed when deployments are usable and trusted by the business that relies on them,” he said. “The sophistication of the model matters far less.”

Data governance must extend across the AI lifecycle

Beyond infrastructure, Retmi said data readiness requires governance to extend from training datasets through inference, model outputs and long-term retention.

Training and fine-tuning depend on datasets that are accurate, consistent, traceable and properly versioned. Organisations must also protect proprietary information, model weights and the applications built around them.

The challenge grows more complex as agentic AI systems take actions across applications and environments, increasing the frequency with which data moves between models and systems.

Organisations therefore need to understand how information is accessed and processed at every stage, which models handle it, where those models operate and who can access the resulting information.

Retmi said Core42’s partnership with Data Dynamics, integrated with Core42 Insight on Sovereign Public Cloud, provides classification, governance and remediation capabilities to help UAE organisations prepare data for AI workloads.

At Gisec 2026, Core42 announced a collaboration with the Technology Innovation Institute to develop and evaluate UAE-built capabilities, including confidential computing and encrypted AI inference, for Sovereign Public Cloud and Compass, Core42’s generative and agentic AI platform.

Long-term retention also requires defined policies for training datasets, model artefacts, generated outputs and associated logs. Retention periods must reflect regulatory obligations, data sensitivity and business requirements, with controls covering storage, access, archiving and secure deletion.

Matching AI workloads to infrastructure

As demand for AI grows across the Gulf, organisations face competing requirements around storage capacity, energy consumption, infrastructure costs and datacentre footprint.

Retmi said the G42 Intelligence Grid distributes responsibilities across specialist providers. Khazna manages the datacentre layer, including power, cooling and physical footprint, while Core42 provides the sovereign-enabled cloud and AI infrastructure. Other partners supply cloud services, accelerators and storage technologies.

Core42 AI Cloud supports accelerators from Nvidia, AMD, Qualcomm and Cerebras, enabling organisations to match workloads to different performance and cost requirements rather than relying on a single hardware architecture.

Retmi cited Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) as an example. The university trains models including Jais, K2 and Jais Climate on Core42 AI Cloud, using different accelerator configurations based on research requirements.

AMD infrastructure can support large exploratory research workloads, while Nvidia H100 clusters can be allocated to frontier-scale training. A common control platform allows workloads to be submitted across the heterogeneous environment, with capacity adjusted to research demand.

This approach is intended to reduce the risk of overprovisioning, where expensive infrastructure sits idle, and underprovisioning, where insufficient capacity creates bottlenecks.

Storage requires a similar balance, Retmi said. High-performance storage should sit close to computing resources for training and inference, while less frequently accessed information can move to lower-cost storage tiers. This helps prevent growth in stored data from translating directly into equivalent increases in energy consumption, costs and physical space.

Large-scale training, foundation model optimisation and fine-tuning can be concentrated where performance and economics are most favourable, while inference can be delivered closer to the point of consumption where required.

“The starting point is matching each workload to the right infrastructure,” Retmi said, noting that not every application needs the largest model, the most powerful accelerator or a real-time response.

Hybrid AI brings new storage requirements

The growing use of hybrid and on-premise AI infrastructure alongside cloud services is also changing storage architecture priorities. Traditional cloud-first environments often relied on centralised cloud storage and managed services. Hybrid deployments add more complexity because data must move between environments with different performance, security and sovereignty requirements.

Retmi said organisations must decide not only where data resides, but also how it moves between systems and remains accessible without creating unnecessary copies or fragmented data silos.

Sensitivity, regulation, latency and operational requirements should determine whether a workload runs on-premise, in a sovereign-enabled public cloud or in a more isolated private environment.

Maintaining consistency across those environments is particularly challenging. Separate infrastructure stacks for each regulatory requirement can increase operational costs and make scaling more difficult. Organisations instead need consistent storage interfaces, access controls and governance policies, along with secure mechanisms for transferring and synchronising data.

Core42’s Signature Private Cloud, powered by Red Hat, provides an open hybrid cloud foundation across connected, restricted and air-gapped environments, according to Retmi.

AI workloads also place different demands on storage performance. Training requires high-throughput access to large datasets to keep accelerators occupied, while inference often prioritises low-latency access to models and supporting information.

Design resilience into the architecture from the outset. Backups and replicas need to remain within the appropriate sovereign boundaries, and recovery plans must be tested regularly.

For Retmi, sovereignty therefore extends beyond the physical location of a datacentre to encompass the full lifecycle of information, from its initial classification and processing through to storage, movement and recovery.

“That is what sovereignty by design means in practice: deciding where data lives, moves and recovers before the first workload goes live,” he added.

title: AI accelerates path from IT compromise to OT targeting
raw_text:
Commercial AI is not yet inventing novel ways to disrupt industrial processes. It is helping non-specialist attackers interpret unfamiliar environments and operationalise known techniques far faster, shrinking the time defenders have to act.

For decades, the complexity of Operational Technology (OT) environments acted as an unintended barrier to entry. Attacking a utility or factory required specialist knowledge of control-system behaviour and how digital interference might carry into a physical process. That expertise was scarce, which kept the population of attackers capable of operating in OT comparatively small.

Complexity was never a security control – it did, however, decide who could turn up and AI is eroding that. It can translate unfamiliar documentation and turn reconnaissance into usable attack paths. It does not turn a generalist into an OT engineer, but it can bring one to the edge of an operational environment faster.

What Monterrey showed

This is not a forecast. Between late December 2025 and mid-February 2026, a single operator used Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's GPT-4.1 as core operational tools in a campaign that compromised nine Mexican government organisations. Gambit Security recovered the forensic material and asked Dragos to examine Servicios de Agua y Drenaje de Monterrey, the municipal water and drainage utility serving the metropolitan area.

We analysed more than 350 recovered artefacts, predominantly AI-generated malicious scripts. Claude Code handled much of the planning and technical execution while GPT-4.1 processed collected data into structured intelligence. Neither model invented new industrial attack capability. They let one operator absorb an unfamiliar environment and apply ordinary techniques at unusual speed.

After the utility's enterprise IT environment was compromised, Claude Code mapped the internal network. It identified a server hosting a vNode industrial gateway and a SCADA/IIoT platform. The model recognised the gateway's significance and analysed its single-password authentication interface. It researched vendor documentation, then generated default and victim-specific credential candidates for an automated password spray. The attempt failed, and we observed no evidence that the adversary breached the OT environment.

The dangerous mistake is to read the case as either nothing or everything. To dismiss it as ordinary automation ignores the way AI supplied missing context while, on the other hand, to call it an autonomous attack assigns the models capabilities they did not show. Both readings miss the point. AI shortened the path from an IT foothold to a credible attempt against OT-adjacent infrastructure and the difficulty of understanding an OT environment was luck, not design.

AI-enabled access, not AI-enabled effect

What we observed was AI-enabled access, not AI-enabled effect. Here, access describes Stage 1 activity in the SANS ICS Cyber Kill Chain: intrusion and discovery within IT, followed by an attempt to reach OT.

The activity did not cross into Stage 2, where an adversary develops and executes a capability intended to affect the physical process. Nothing we recovered demonstrated novel OT tradecraft or the engineering knowledge required for that effect as the models operationalised public information and known techniques, while attribution remains unresolved.

The meaningful compression was in tooling development and interpretation. Work that would have taken days or weeks was completed in hours. The operator arrived without a prior OT objective or specialist knowledge.

The relevant boundary is operational consequence

AI is shortening the route to the door but it has not removed what lies beyond it. A deliberate physical effect still requires process-specific engineering knowledge. Dragos uses extended operational technology, or xOT, as the standard for defining that environment. Any system that influences a physical process or drives a high-impact operational outcome sits inside it, whatever its conventional classification. The label matters less than the consequence. Power grids, water systems, manufacturing plants, pipelines and data centres all depend on specialised technologies and on engineering decisions taken long before any of this was in prospect.

The consequences are easy to misclassify. Our 2026 OT Cybersecurity Year in Review tracked 119 ransomware groups targeting OT organisations during 2025, up 49% on the 80 tracked in 2024. Around 3,300 organisations were affected, with manufacturing accounting for more than two-thirds of victims. When attackers encrypt a Windows engineering workstation or a human-machine interface, the incident is usually logged as an IT problem. It rarely is one, and this misclassification is why the reported operational impact of ransomware sits below the real one. Recovery is not a reimage either as teams must verify the configuration and safety functions before returning the process to a known state.

The 2025 OT Security Financial Risk Report, produced for Dragos by the Marsh McLennan Cyber Risk Intelligence Center, puts figures on the exposure. In a typical year, OT-related incidents represent around $31.1bn of modelled global financial risk. In a severe but plausible one-in-250-year scenario that rises to $329.5bn, and more than half of it is business interruption rather than data loss.

Defenders need to win the time-to-decision race

The same technology can be worth more to defenders, but only when grounded in OT-specific context. Attackers can work from public documentation and network data but defenders hold the ground truth about what each asset does and which dependencies carry operational consequence. They know the process limits and safety constraints.

This is the problem we designed the Dragos Intelligence Fabric and Dragos EmberAI to address. The Intelligence Fabric connects OT asset knowledge and frontline threat intelligence with the organisation's own environment while Dragos EmberAI gives analysts a plain-language route into that context. Which assets are talking over a given protocol? Which vulnerabilities warrant the next patch window, judged on adversary behaviour and operational impact rather than a raw CVSS score? The analyst still makes the decision, and the evidence behind each answer stays auditable.

Organisations should start by mapping paths to consequence, not merely compiling an asset list. The map must include identity and remote-access infrastructure as well as gateways and vendor connections. Architecture must stop an IT foothold from becoming an OT problem in an afternoon. Every route across the boundary should be visible and tightly controlled, with deliberate segmentation. In the UK and Europe that work now carries regulatory weight. NIS2 and the NCSC's Cyber Assessment Framework both expect operators to show they understand their operational dependencies and can respond to an intrusion, and neither is satisfied by an asset register.

Operational context and response roles must also be current before an intrusion begins. No model can manufacture trustworthy context from stale spreadsheets during a crisis. The same modelling puts an OT-specific incident-response plan at up to an 18.5% average reduction in financial risk, with defensible architecture and network visibility close behind. Preparedness changes the outcome.

The harder requirement is speed. The new race is between the adversary's time-to-understanding and the defender's time-to-decision. In Monterrey, a single operator using commercial models moved from an IT foothold to an attempt against an industrial gateway in hours. A defender working from prose reports and disconnected dashboards is not operating on that clock.

AI is compressing the time an intrusion needs to reach an operational system, and geopolitical pressure has put critical infrastructure in front of a wider set of adversaries than at any point in my career. Monterrey should be read in both directions before reaching for the alarm - and while complexity is no longer a reliable barrier, engineering fundamentals remain one.

What Stage 2 looks like

In January 2024, attackers used the malware to manipulate ENCO control systems through legitimate Modbus commands at a municipal district energy company in Lviv, Ukraine, leaving more than 600 apartment buildings without heating for almost two days in sub-zero temperatures.

FrostyGoop, as it was named, was not an AI case, and the code was never the hard part. It is a Modbus client, and our own research has shown that a model will produce something equivalent on request. What a model will not supply is the knowledge that downgrading the controller firmware removes the operator's view, or that reporting cold water as hot stops a heating system. That is process-specific engineering knowledge, and it remains the boundary.

FrostyGoop is a reminder of what Stage 2 means and what defenders are protecting – and the consequence was not lost data, it was people in the cold.

Magpie Graham is vice-president, strategic intelligence, Dragos.

title: Suspect Post Office systems that came before Horizon to be investigated by the government
raw_text:
The government expects to report on the impact of pre-Horizon software system errors on subpostmasters by spring next year.

It said it is currently looking for an investigation firm to carry out the work, announced earlier this week, which will look at the wider impact multiple software systems had on subpostmasters’ businesses and lives.

“We are yet to finalise the scope of the investigation as a supplier has not yet been selected. We will be looking at a range of software and systems in place that pre-date Horizon,” said the government.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) has already stated that it is looking into multiple Post Office software systems that are potentially implicated in the miscarriages of justice suffered by subpostmasters.

Now, through the new investigation, the government plans to get a “fuller understanding” of these systems and “their impact” on subpostmasters.

The Post Office scandal was triggered by, but not caused by, software errors. It was the result of the Post Office’s policy of making subpostmasters pay for unexplained shortfalls that appeared on branch accounting systems. This policy did not just exist for Horizon but had in fact existed for many years and applied to unexplained shortfalls on any system used by subpostmasters.

The CCRC told MPs in January that there are 35 applications of interest, which it refers to as “pre-Horizon”. It said that any of these systems could be linked to miscarriages of justice, and it is not a giant leap to suggest that pre-Horizon software also caused unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to cover.

Pre-Horizon systems of note include Capture, ECCO+, Automated Payment Service (APS)/Automated Payment Technology (APT) and ALPS/OBCS.

Read more about ECCO+: Post Office acknowledges ECCO+ user’s calls for help three decades ago.

Although the Capture system was used before Horizon, an investigation has already established its flaws, therefore it will not be included in the latest investigation, the government told Computer Weekly.

The establishment of Capture’s errors in an investigation by Kroll in 2024 ultimately contributed to the establishment of a compensation scheme, separate to those related to Horizon, for former Capture users. The CCRC began reviewing convictions based on data from the software and has so far referred two convictions based on Capture data to the Court of Appeal, with more being reviewed.

A conviction based on the APT/APS system was also referred to the Court of Appeal in December 2025. The 2001 conviction of former subpostmaster Gareth Snow was passed to the appeal court after the CCRC established that there was evidence that the APS/APT, which Snow used in his branch in Denbighshire, “could cause accounting errors”.

But the current cases and systems being reviewed “may represent just the tip of another iceberg”, said a select committee report in March. During the 1980s and 1990s, multiple systems were used in Post Offices to automate work before the introduction of the Horizon system. These early systems were susceptible to errors that users and the Post Office did not understand. In the same way as with Horizon, subpostmasters were contractually obliged to take responsibility for unexplained losses.

The CCRC has identified what it describes as 35 “pre-Horizon applications”.

The government said: “Consistent with our approach to the Capture software, an independent investigator will establish a fuller understanding of those software applications and their impact, providing government with a robust evidence base to inform any future considerations.”

summary:
The government expects to report on the impact of pre-Horizon software system errors on subpostmasters by spring next year.

It said it is currently looking for an investigation firm to carry out the work, announced earlier this week, which will look at the wider impact multiple software systems had on subpostmasters’ businesses and lives.

“We are yet to finalise the scope of the investigation as a supplier has not yet been selected. We will be looking at a range of software and systems in place that pre-date Horizon,” said the government.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) has already stated that it is looking into multiple Post Office software systems that are potentially implicated in the miscarriages of justice suffered by subpostmasters.

Now, through the new investigation, the government plans to get a “fuller understanding” of these systems and “their impact” on subpostmasters.

The Post Office scandal was triggered by, but not caused by, software errors. It was the result of the Post Office’s policy of making subpostmasters pay for unexplained shortfalls that appeared on branch accounting systems. This policy did not just exist for Horizon but had in fact existed for many years and applied to unexplained shortfalls on any system used by subpostmasters.

The CCRC told MPs in January that there are 35 applications of interest, which it refers to as “pre-Horizon”.

title: Botched PHP2Shell disclosure revealed as panic continues
raw_text:
A worldwide cyber panic sparked by the discovery and disclosure of two critical vulnerabilities – dubbed PHP2Shell – in the core PHP code underpinning almost three-quarters of the world’s websites has sparked widespread commentary and debate in the cyber security community after the disclosure process went horribly wrong.

As already reported, the artificial intelligence (AI-)discovered flaws in the 32-year-old PHP server-side language enable unauthenticated threat actors to attain remote code execution (RCE) capabilities on affected servers given certain conditions.

An emergency patch dropped on Wednesday 21 October addressing both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, but it has now emerged that thanks to a series of unfortunate events, the disclosure process ended up being somewhat botched.

The PHP Foundation said that work had been ongoing on disclosure since August and this had been working well until the afternoon of Tuesday 20 October, when the two CVE designations assigned to the vulnerabilities began to circulate online accompanied by misinformation about their planned release and severity.

This leak forced the PHP Foundation to move up its timeline with the release moving forward by approximately 24 hours. As a result of this, cyber firm Calif, whose researchers first flagged one of the flaws and had been working on the coordinated disclosure process with the PHP Foundation, mistakenly released a video it had prepared showing a proof of concept in action and revealing some key details about the vulnerabilities. This quickly made its way to social media and accelerated the development of other exploits.

The PHP Foundation added that mitigation advice given to critical infrastructure providers may also have leaked, but the final straw came when a company which had had early access to enable its users to immediately apply the patch released built images containing the fix

In a write-up of the incident, the PHP Foundation accused Chainguard, an open source cyber specialist, of unilaterally breaking the embargo on PHP2Shell.

“Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” wrote the PHP Foundation.

Writing on LinkedIn, Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc acknowledged the company’s role in the process. He said: “The PHP Foundation and maintainers did an amazing job here in a high-stress situation. I’m sorry that my decision led to even more stress for them.”

Lorenc explained he took the decision to ship the patch early after noting spreading online gossip and coordinating with other researchers. “This decision was based on how easily we were able to independently discover the vulnerability and build an exploit, how much information was already out there on the coming vulnerabilities and fixes, and the evidence shared on active exploits in the wild,” he said.

Lorenc added: “We’re all on one team here, trying to minimise harm on end users from attacks … We’re not always going to get it right, and not everyone is going to agree with our decisions, but that is always our goal. This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry.”

John Bruggeman, virtual chief information security officer (vCISO) at IT services house CBTS, described coordinated disclosure as a trust exercise: “The bad news is that this week someone let go of the rope.

“An embargo isn’t a formality. It’s the only mechanism the security community has for giving defenders a head start over attackers on something this widespread. It only works if every party holding early access treats ‘early’ as ‘early for patching’, not ‘early for publishing’. 

“One broken link, and the thing that was supposed to protect millions of PHP servers becomes the thing that tips attackers off faster,” said Bruggeman. “What this means for security leaders is that you need to be able to patch fast, sometimes faster than you’ve planned, even if you’re on the inside.”

Mind-boggling scale of disruption

In the UK, the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are already known to have affected multiple central and local government bodies, which have been forced to pull services offline, as well as the BBC. Given the extent to which web services – particularly ecommerce operations – rely on PHP, thousands of other private sector organisations will inevitably be affected.

And the scale of the potential disruption is mind-boggling. According to figures provided by Qualys’ Threat Research Unit (TRU), there are hundreds of millions of PHP package installations in the wild, with almost three-quarters of them on internet-facing assets leaving them within range of remote attackers.

To make matters worse, the available patches only cover versions 8.2 and newer of PHP, leaving millions of websites relying on older versions dangerously exposed, and dramatically widening the scope of the incident.

Thankfully, with the PHP2Shell incident having received extensive publicity, patching rates are thought to be increasingly rapidly, with a live tracker provided by UK-based cyber startup Infrawatch showing that as of approximately 20:20 UTC on Thursday 22 October, almost 140,000 visible PHP instances had been patched, rising at a rate of around 7,000 every hour.

However, according to Infrawatch, this represents barely 6% (8.5% in the UK) of the publicly visible total, and as of late afternoon on Thursday 22 October, a surge in attempted exploitation of the two PHP flaws is being widely observed – and, according to Amazon’s threat intel researchers, may have been ongoing since at least 17 October.

According to the PHP Foundation, the two flaws are particularly dangerous because they sit in parts of PHP – memory management and error handling – that virtually every request makes.

“Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions,” said the PHP Foundation.

The PHP Foundation said CVE-2026-109618 arises from an out-of-memory corruption condition. Should a request reach PHP’s memory limit at the wrong moment, it could leave partially initialised internal data behind and later assume it to be valid, corrupting the memory. In some circumstances, an unauthenticated request could trigger this situation before any application code runs, enabling RCE to take place.

CVE-2026-109691 arises from a stale global state condition. In this situation, a fatal error at an inopportune moment leaves internal state pointing to memory belonging to a previous request. If the same worker then handles a later request, it could then use that memory, leading to what is known as a use-after-free condition, and a crash, also enabling RCE.

For Sai Molige, senior manager of threat hunting at Forescout, the PHP2Shell incident has the potential to become an event on the same scale as the 2021 Log4Shell incident affecting the Apache Log4j library, but not for quite the same reason.

“With Log4j, the main problem was finding a library you didn’t know you had. With PHP, much of the forgotten infrastructure will be found, but won’t have an upstream fix,” he explained. “The durable lesson from Log4j is that organisations should treat ‘How quickly can we identify where we run X?’ as a measurable capability separate from patching speed.

“Discovering vulnerable infrastructure, however, is only the first step. When older systems have no available fix or depend on a vendor update, organisations need to reduce exposure, restrict unnecessary connections and isolate affected systems while planning remediation.”

title: BMW uses Ansible to manage HPC cluster
raw_text:
BMW Group has migrated its high-performance computing (HPC) cluster comprising 15,000 Windows and Linux servers to the Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform to improve manageability and IT automation. The Red Hat platform also enables self-service, reducing the IT admin time needed to deploy applications for users.

The HPC infrastructure is used in performance-intensive applications such as 3D modelling, crash test simulations and new car design. 

For the past 30 years, the HPC environment has been managed by a custom application known as scVenus, which needed replacing as it neared end-of-life.

The German carmaker, which owns brands including Mini, BMW and Rolls-Royce, assessed the Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform and worked with the Red Hat technical account management team, along with partners including IBM and Puzzle ITC AG, on the migration of applications, servers and client software.

Discussing the migration, Martina Pretzl, project leader for HPC at BMW Group, said: “Replacing a 30-year-old legacy system across 15,000 servers while maintaining continuous vehicle production is a monumental challenge. By collaborating closely with Red Hat and our partners, we operated as a single, unified team to deliver this highly complex migration on time and within budget, establishing a modern, agile automation foundation.”

According to Red Hat, moving to the Ansible Automation Platform has enabled BMW Group to use Ansible Playbooks. This, it said, has enabled complex infrastructure tasks that previously required up to 60 hours of processing time on thousands of nodes to be reduced to just 20 minutes. Other routine management processes have been cut by 75%, from 12 hours to three hours.

BMW Group has also introduced “shift left” self-service capabilities through a unified self-service portal to enable users to manage their own software licence restarts and support requests.

The car manufacturer has also deployed infrastructure as code for resilience. This enables redundancy and automated disaster recovery across thousands of endpoints and multiple availability zones.

Looking ahead, the IT team at BMW Group plans to introduce event-driven automation to resolve routine IT service issues automatically. BMW Group is also transitioning towards a more cloud-native, containerised architecture, and plans to use AI coding assistants alongside the Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform’s automated policy as code, enabling faster development while maintaining strict compliance.

Johan Barnard, team lead for Ansible Core at BMW Group, said: “Red Hat Ansible Automation will be with us for the foreseeable future. AI can’t be trusted directly to run your production systems – you need automation as that trust layer.”

Earlier this year, BMW Group progressed its cloud-first strategy with NTT Data’s managed services for its global network, across 40,000 network devices, 260,000 ports and 30,000 servers.

In 2022, it began working with HPE to use the company’s GreenLake edge-to-cloud IT infrastructure to provide cloud services for big data, backup, recovery and compliant archiving for the development of electric vehicles. The HPE technology has enabled BMW Group to manage distributed data via a single platform, with a globally consistent cloud experience.

It is also a reference customer for Amazon Web Services, and has been collaborating with the public cloud service provider to develop commercial off-the-shelf cloud technology for securely managing vehicle data.
